claim: The insulin-like signaling pathway maintains a relatively short wild-type lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans by phosphorylating and inactivating DAF-16.
source: The insulin-like signaling pathway maintains a relatively short wild-type lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans by phosphorylating and inactivating DAF-16, the ortholog of the FOXO transcription factors of mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Kenyon et al., 1993; Morris et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1997).

claim: DAF-16 is the ortholog of the FOXO transcription factors of mammalian cells.
source: The insulin-like signaling pathway maintains a relatively short wild-type lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans by phosphorylating and inactivating DAF-16, the ortholog of the FOXO transcription factors of mammalian cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary relationship between C. elegans DAF-16 and mammalian FOXO proteins.

claim: DAF-16 is phosphorylated by the AKT kinases, preventing its nuclear translocation.
source: DAF-16 is phosphorylated by the AKT kinases, preventing its nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by established literature and experimental data in the manuscript (Lin et al., 2001).

claim: Calcineurin (PP2B phosphatase) limits the lifespan of C. elegans.
source: Calcineurin (PP2B phosphatase) also limits the lifespan of C. elegans, but the mechanism through which it does so is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript (Dong et al., 2007).

claim: TAX-6•CNB-1 and UNC-43 regulate lifespan through DAF-16.
source: Herein, we show that TAX-6•CNB-1 and UNC-43, the C. elegans Calcineurin and Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase type II (CAMKII) orthologs, respectively, also regulate lifespan through DAF-16.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by genetic and biochemical experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: UNC-43 regulates DAF-16 in response to starvation, heat stress, and oxidative stress.
source: Moreover, UNC-43 regulates DAF-16 in response to various stress conditions, including starvation, heat or oxidative stress, and cooperatively contributes to lifespan regulation by insulin signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing DAF-16 nuclear localization under stress conditions in wild-type but not unc-43(null) animals (Figure 6G).

claim: UNC-43 phosphorylates and activates DAF-16, promoting its nuclear localization.
source: However, unlike insulin signaling, UNC-43 phosphorylates and activates DAF-16, thus promoting its nuclear localization.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays, mass spectrometry, and localization studies shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: UNC-43 phosphorylates DAF-16 at S286.
source: The phosphorylation of DAF-16 at S286 by UNC-43 is removed by TAX-6•CNB-1, leading to DAF-16 inactivation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry (Figure 5A), in vitro kinase assays (Figure 5B-C), and in vivo immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5D).

claim: TAX-6•CNB-1 removes the phosphorylation at S286 of DAF-16, leading to DAF-16 inactivation.
source: The phosphorylation of DAF-16 at S286 by UNC-43 is removed by TAX-6•CNB-1, leading to DAF-16 inactivation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro phosphatase assays showing TAX-6•CNB-1 reduces S286 phosphorylation (Figure 5F).

claim: Mammalian FOXO3 is regulated by CAMKIIA and Calcineurin.
source: Mammalian FOXO3 is also regulated by CAMKIIA and Calcineurin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 9B-C), in vitro kinase assays (Figure 9D-F), and luciferase reporter assays (Figure 10).

claim: The IIS pathway is the best characterized pathway regulating aging in C. elegans.
source: The best characterized is the IIS pathway, which includes the upstream insulin/IGF-1 receptor DAF-2 and the downstream FOXO transcription factor DAF-16.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by extensive literature (Kenyon, 2005; Greer and Brunet, 2008).

claim: Signals from DAF-2 are transmitted through AGE-1, PDK-1 to AKT-1, AKT-2, and SGK-1.
source: Signals from DAF-2 are transmitted through AGE-1 (phosphoinositide 3-kinase) and PDK-1 (phosphoinositol-dependent kinase-1) to AKT-1, AKT-2, and SGK-1, which phosphorylate DAF-16 and prevent it from translocating to the nucleus to activate a pro-longevity gene network.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the insulin signaling pathway in C. elegans.

claim: Reduction-of-function mutations of kinase genes in the IIS pathway extend lifespan in a daf-16-dependent manner.
source: Reduction-of-function mutations of the kinase genes in the IIS pathway, from daf-2 to akt-1, akt-2, and sgk-1, all extend lifespan in a daf-16-dependent manner (Kenyon et al., 1993; Morris et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1997; Hertweck et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Lifespan extension by reduced IIS is conserved in flies and mice.
source: Lifespan extension by reduced IIS is also observed in other species, including flies and mice, indicating that the pathway is conserved evolutionarily (Kenyon, 2005; Greer and Brunet, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on evolutionary conservation of the IIS pathway.

claim: PPTR-1 is a B56 regulatory subunit of PP2A that directs PP2A to dephosphorylate AKT-1 at T350.
source: The only known example is PPTR-1, a B56 regulatory subunit of PP2A, which directs PP2A to dephosphorylate AKT-1 at T350, thereby inactivating the kinase (Padmanabhan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: DAF-18 is the C. elegans PTEN and is a phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) 3-phosphatase.
source: DAF-18, the C. elegans PTEN, is a phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) 3-phosphatase (Ogg and Ruvkun, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants for tax-6 and cnb-1 live longer than wild-type worms.
source: Previously, loss-of-function (lf) mutants for tax-6 and cnb-1, which encode the catalytic and regulatory subunits of C. elegans Calcineurin, respectively, were found to live longer than wild-type (WT) worms (Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Calcineurin (PP2B) is a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein phosphatase in mammalian systems.
source: In mammalian systems, Calcineurin (PP2B) is a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein phosphatase that has diverse functions and affects both T cell activation and heart development (Crabtree, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian Calcineurin, supported by citation.

claim: In C. elegans, Calcineurin regulates body size, thermotaxis, muscle contraction, and lifespan.
source: In C. elegans, Calcineurin regulates body size, thermotaxis, muscle contraction, and lifespan (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2002; Kuhara et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2004; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The longevity phenotype of tax-6(lf) is partially dependent on daf-16.
source: The longevity phenotype of tax-6(lf) is partially dependent on daf-16 (Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: C. elegans Calcineurin can regulate lifespan by suppressing autophagy.
source: More recent studies have shown that C. elegans Calcineurin can regulate lifespan by suppressing autophagy (Dwivedi et al., 2009) or inactivating CRTC-1, a co-activator of CREB (Mair et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: C. elegans Calcineurin can regulate lifespan by inactivating CRTC-1, a co-activator of CREB.
source: More recent studies have shown that C. elegans Calcineurin can regulate lifespan by suppressing autophagy (Dwivedi et al., 2009) or inactivating CRTC-1, a co-activator of CREB (Mair et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: TAX-6 and DAF-16 interact with each other in vivo.
source: This result suggested that TAX-6 and DAF-16 interacted with each other in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TAX-6•GST-CNB-1 directly binds to His-tagged DAF-16.
source: Indeed, TAX-6•GST-CNB-1 was pulled down successfully using His-tagged DAF-16 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays with purified recombinant proteins shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The C-terminal region of DAF-16 mediates the interaction with Calcineurin.
source: Further analysis suggested that the C-terminal region of DAF-16 mediates the interaction with Calcineurin (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays with DAF-16 fragments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DAF-16::6xHis::GFP accumulates in the nuclei of different types of cells in tax-6(ok2065).
source: DAF-16::6xHis::GFP clearly accumulated in the nuclei of different types of cells in tax-6(ok2065) (Figure 1D), similar to daf-2(lf) and akt-1;akt-2(RNAi) mutants (Henderson and Johnson, 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1D.

claim: unc-43 RNAi abolished DAF-16 nuclear accumulation in tax-6(ok2065).
source: The suppression was confirmed by an independent, homemade unc-43 RNAi construct (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: unc-43 encodes the only Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase, type II (CAMKII), in C. elegans.
source: The unc-43 gene encodes the only Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein kinase, type II (CAMKII), in C. elegans (Reiner et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: UNC-43 and Calcineurin have opposing functions in locomotion and egg laying.
source: UNC-43 and Calcineurin have opposing functions in locomotion and egg laying, two behavioral phenotypes that are regulated by G protein signaling (Reiner et al., 1999; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: unc-43(lf);cnb-1(null) double mutant animals arrest at the L1 larval stage.
source: However, they also have non-overlapping functions because unc-43(lf);cnb-1(null) double mutant animals arrest at the L1 larval stage, whereas both single mutants are viable (Reiner et al., 1999; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Adult stage RNAi knockdown of tax-6 extended the WT lifespan.
source: Adult stage RNAi knockdown of tax-6 extended the WT lifespan (p=0.001) (B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: tax-6 RNAi may have slightly shortened the lifespan of unc-43(n498n1186), a putative null mutant.
source: but may have slightly shortened the lifespan of unc-43(n498n1186), a putative null mutant (p=0.04) (C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: unc-43(n498), a constitutively active gain-of-function mutation, caused DAF-16::6xHis::GFP to accumulate in the nucleus.
source: A constitutively active gain-of-function mutation, unc-43(n498), caused DAF-16::6xHis::GFP to accumulate in the nucleus (D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2D.

claim: unc-43(n498) extended lifespan in a largely daf-16-dependent manner.
source: and extended lifespan in a largely daf-16-dependent manner (E). p<0.001 for daf-16(mu86);unc-43(gf) vs daf-16(mu86) or unc-43(gf).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The unc-43(gf);cnb-1(null) double mutant has a longer lifespan than both the unc-43(gf) and cnb-1(null) mutants.
source: (F) The unc-43(gf);cnb-1(null) double mutant has a longer lifespan than both the unc-43(gf) and cnb-1(null) mutants, and all three mutant strains live longer than WT animals. p<0.001 for WT vs any mutant, and p<0.001 for unc-43(gf);cnb-1(null) vs unc-43(gf) and cnb-1(null).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: RNAi knockdown of nsy-1, sek-1, and pmk-2 failed to block the nuclear accumulation of DAF-16::6xHis::GFP in unc-43(gf) mutants.
source: (A) RNAi knockdown of nsy-1, sek-1, and pmk-2 failed to block the nuclear accumulation of DAF-16::6xHis::GFP in unc-43(gf) mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sek-1(km4) mutation did not eliminate DAF-16 nuclear localization in unc-43(gf) worms.
source: (B) Similar to sek-1 RNAi, the sek-1(km4) mutation did not eliminate DAF-16 nuclear localization in unc-43(gf) worms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: km4, a null allele of sek-1, did not shorten the lifespan of WT or unc-43(gf) animals.
source: (C) km4, a null allele of sek-1, did not shorten the lifespan of WT or unc-43(gf) animals. In contrast, km4 may have slightly extended their lifespan. p=0.001 for sek-1(null) vs WT and p=0.047 for unc-43(gf); sek-1(null) vs unc-43(gf).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 3xHA::UNC-43 co-immunoprecipitated with 3xFLAG::DAF-16 from lysates of transgenic C. elegans expressing both proteins.
source: The 3xHA::UNC-43 protein was found in the immunoprecipitate of 3xFLAG::DAF-16 and vice versa (Figure 4A–B), suggesting that UNC-43 and DAF-16 can form a complex in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: GST-UNC-43 was pulled down by nickel beads via 6xHis-DAF-16.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we found that GST-UNC-43 but not GST or calmodulin (CAM), was pulled down by nickel beads via 6xHis-DAF-16 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays with purified recombinant proteins shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GST-UNC-43 directly phosphorylated His-tagged DAF-16 in vitro.
source: GST-UNC-43 readily phosphorylated DAF-16 in vitro (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: UNC-43 phosphorylated the DAF-16 N-F fragment (1–267 aa) but not the N-terminal fragment (1–142 aa).
source: UNC-43 phosphorylated the DAF-16 N-F fragment (1–267 aa) but not the N-terminal fragment (1–142 aa) (Figure 4E), suggesting that the phosphorylation site(s) resides in the region containing the forkhead domain (143–267 aa) and/or the C-terminal region (268–508 aa).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays with DAF-16 fragments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified two DAF-16 residues T240 and S286 that were phosphorylated by UNC-43.
source: A mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the full-length 6xHis-DAF-16 after the in vitro kinase reaction identified two DAF-16 residues T240 and S286 that were phosphorylated by UNC-43 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DAF-16 was phosphorylated by UNC-43 at T240 and S286 in vitro.
source: Using these antibodies, we verified that DAF-16 was indeed phosphorylated by UNC-43 at T240 and S286 in vitro (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blots with phospho-specific antibodies shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: There was a marked increase of DAF-16 S286 phosphorylation, but not T240 phosphorylation, in the unc-43(gf) mutant.
source: Interestingly, there was a marked increase of DAF-16 S286 phosphorylation, but not T240 phosphorylation, in the unc-43(gf) mutant (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot experiments shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: UNC-43 phosphorylates DAF-16 specifically on S286 in vivo.
source: We thus concluded that UNC-43 phosphorylates DAF-16 specifically on S286.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that S286 phosphorylation increases in unc-43(gf) mutants while T240 phosphorylation does not (Figure 5D-E).

claim: T240 phosphorylation by UNC-43 does not occur in vivo under the tested condition.
source: Apparently, T240 phosphorylation by UNC-43 does not occur in vivo under the tested condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increased T240 phosphorylation in unc-43(gf) mutants (Figure 5E).

claim: Phosphorylation of DAF-16 at S286 was dramatically reduced by TAX-6•GST-CNB-1.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, phosphorylation of DAF-16 at S286 was dramatically reduced by TAX-6•GST-CNB-1, while phosphorylation of T240 remained unchanged.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro phosphatase assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DAF-16(S286A)::6xHis::GFP distributed diffusely throughout the cell in tax-6(lf) and unc-43(gf) mutant backgrounds.
source: While DAF-16::6xHis::GFP accumulated in the nuclei of tax-6(lf) and unc-43(gf) mutants, DAF-16(S286A)::6xHis::GFP distributed diffusely throughout the cell in the same mutant backgrounds (Figure 6A–B), and the pattern resembled that of DAF-16::6xHis::GFP in WT worms (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The lifespan extension by either unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf) was greatly suppressed in C. elegans whose WT copy of DAF-16 was replaced by DAF-16(S286A).
source: In C. elegans whose WT copy of DAF-16 was replaced by DAF-16(S286A), the lifespan extension by either unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf) was greatly suppressed (Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—source data 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The S286 residue is required for DAF-16-dependent effects of unc-43(gf) and tax-6(lf).
source: Thus, the S286 residue is required for DAF-16-dependent effects of unc-43(gf) and tax-6(lf), verifying that S286 is the regulatory site.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that S286A mutation blocks the effects of unc-43(gf) and tax-6(lf) on DAF-16 localization and lifespan (Figure 6A-D).

claim: DAF-16(S286D)::6xHis::GFP accumulated in the nucleus when expressed in daf-16(mu86) animals.
source: When expressed in daf-16(mu86) animals, the DAF-16(S286D)::6xHis::GFP protein accumulated in the nucleus, whereas the WT DAF-16::6xHis::GFP protein was cytoplasmic, as expected (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The phosphomimetic of DAF-16 (S286D), but not the WT version, significantly increased the C. elegans lifespan in daf-16(null) animals.
source: Moreover, the phosphomimetic of DAF-16, but not the WT version, significantly increased the C. elegans lifespan in daf-16(null) animals (Figure 6F, Figure 6—source data 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Heat stress, oxidative stress, and starvation induced nuclear accumulation of DAF-16::6xHis::GFP in WT animals but not in unc-43(n498n1186) mutants.
source: 2 hr of heat stress at 28°C, 5 min of paraquat treatment, or 20 hr of food deprivation induced nuclear accumulation of DAF-16::6xHis::GFP in the WT animals but not the unc-43(n498n1186) mutants (G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6G.

claim: unc-43 is required for nuclear accumulation of DAF-16 in response to different types of stress.
source: The results demonstrated that unc-43 is required for nuclear accumulation of DAF-16 in response to different types of stress.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that stress-induced DAF-16 nuclear accumulation is blocked in unc-43(null) mutants (Figure 6G).

claim: Reduced IIS and increased phosphorylation of DAF-16 S286 displayed an additive effect on lifespan.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, reduced IIS and increased phosphorylation of DAF-16 S286, either by unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf), displayed an additive effect on lifespan (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—source data 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: An unc-43 null allele shortened the daf-2 lifespan by 31%.
source: First, an unc-43 null allele shortened the daf-2 lifespan by 31% (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1B), indicating that unc-43 is required for full lifespan extension by daf-2(e1370).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: unc-43 is required for full lifespan extension by daf-2(e1370).
source: First, an unc-43 null allele shortened the daf-2 lifespan by 31% (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1B), indicating that unc-43 is required for full lifespan extension by daf-2(e1370).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unc-43(null) shortens daf-2 lifespan (Figure 7C).

claim: In long-lived unc-43(gf) animals, phosphorylation by AKT on T240 is greatly reduced.
source: Second, in the constitutively active unc-43(gf) mutant, which has increased phosphorylation on DAF-16 S286 (Figure 5D), phosphorylation by AKT on T240 is greatly reduced (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: unc-43(gf) reduced the amount of DAF-16-associated 14-3-3 without affecting the total amount of 14-3-3.
source: Consistently, we found that unc-43(gf) reduced the amount of DAF-16-associated 14-3-3 without affecting the total amount of 14-3-3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nuclear DAF-16::GFP was clearly visible above the cytoplasmic background in daf-2(RNAi), daf-2(RNAi);unc-43(null), or daf-2(RNAi);tax-6(gf) mutants.
source: DAF-16::GFP was cytoplasmic in unc-43(null) or tax-6(gf), but nuclear DAF-16::GFP was clearly visible above the cytoplasmic background in daf-2(RNAi), daf-2(RNAi);unc-43(null), or daf-2(RNAi);tax-6(gf) mutants (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The nuclear accumulation induced by unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf) was greatly diminished by daf-18 RNAi.
source: In both cases, the nuclear accumulation induced by unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf) was greatly diminished by daf-18 RNAi (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Under conditions in which there is a conflict between IIS and CAMKII/Calcineurin signaling toward DAF-16, the insulin signaling pathway appears to dominate.
source: Therefore, under conditions in which there is a conflict between IIS and CAMKII/Calcineurin signaling toward DAF-16, the insulin signaling pathway appears to dominate.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that daf-2(RNAi) can override unc-43(null) or tax-6(gf), and daf-18(RNAi) can override unc-43(gf) or tax-6(lf) (Figure 8A-B).

claim: DAF-16 S286 is conserved in nematode species, zebra fish, frogs, mice, and humans.
source: Sequence analysis of FOXO proteins revealed that DAF-16 S286, the CAMKII phosphorylation site, is widely conserved in nematode species, zebra fish, frogs, mice, and humans (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 9A.

claim: DAF-16 S286 is equivalent to S298 of mouse FOXO3 and S299 of human FOXO3.
source: It is equivalent to S298 of mouse FOXO3 (mFOXO3) and S299 of human FOXO3 (hFOXO3) (Figure 9A), and may be the equivalent of S303 of human FOXO1 or S300 of mouse FOXO1 (not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 9A.

claim: FLAG-FOXO3 immunoprecipitation pulled down both CAMKII isoforms.
source: Immunoprecipitation of FLAG-FOXO3 pulled down both CAMKII isoforms (B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: FLAG-FOXO3 immunoprecipitation pulled down Calcineurin.
source: and Calcineurin (C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 9C.

claim: CAMKIIA robustly phosphorylated the P2 and P3 fragments of FOXO3 but not the others.
source: CAMKIIA robustly phosphorylated the P2 and P3 fragments but not the others (Figure 9D), placing the phosphorylation sites within aa 154–409.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Mass spectrometry and mutagenesis studies mapped the CAMKIIA phosphorylation sites to S252, S279, and S298 of mFOXO3.
source: Mass spectrometry and mutagenesis studies of the full-length mFOXO3 or the P2 and P3 fragments from the in vitro kinase assay mapped the CAMKIIA phosphorylation sites to S252, S279, and S298 (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a result of mass spectrometry and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The same sites (S252, S279, and S298) were also identified from FLAG-mFOXO3 co-expressed with CAMKIIA in HEK293T cells.
source: The same sites were also identified from FLAG-mFOXO3 co-expressed with CAMKIIA in HEK293T cells (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only mFOXO3 S298 had a significant increase in phosphorylation when cells were co-transfected with CAMKIIA.
source: However, only mFOXO3 S298, which corresponds to DAF-16 S286, had a significant increase in phosphorylation when cells were co-transfected with CAMKIIA (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: S298 is the principle CAMKIIA phosphorylation site in vivo.
source: This shows that S298 is the principle CAMKIIA phosphorylation site in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that S298 shows the largest increase in phosphorylation upon CAMKIIA co-expression (Figure 9F).

claim: Neither CAMKIIA nor Calcineurin regulated phosphorylation of endogenous human FOXO3 at S253 in HEK293T cells.
source: Using a specific antibody, we found that neither CAMKIIA nor Calcineurin regulated phosphorylation of endogenous human FOXO3 at S253 in HEK293T cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Calcineurin can reduce the phosphorylation of the FOXO3-P3 fragment (containing S298) by CAMKIIA.
source: Moreover, Calcineurin can reduce the phosphorylation of the FOXO3-P3 fragment (containing S298) by CAMKIIA, but not that of the P2 fragment (containing S252) (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro phosphatase assays shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mammalian CAMKII and Calcineurin regulate phosphorylation of FOXO3 at the same conserved site as in C. elegans (S298 in mouse FOXO3 and S286 in DAF-16).
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that mammalian CAMKII and Calcineurin regulate phosphorylation of FOXO3 at the same conserved site as in C. elegans (S298 in mouse FOXO3 and S286 in DAF-16).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results showing that CAMKIIA phosphorylates FOXO3 at S298 and Calcineurin dephosphorylates this site (Figures 9 and 10).

claim: The transcriptional activity of FOXO3 was stimulated by CAMKIIA in a way that required S298 of FOXO3.
source: Using a luciferase reporter assay, we found that the transcriptional activity of FOXO3 was indeed stimulated by CAMKIIA in a way that required S298 of FOXO3 (Figure 10A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The transcriptional activity of FOXO3 stimulation by CAMKIIA required T286 of CAMKIIA.
source: and T286 of CAMKIIA (Figure 10B),
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The transcriptional activity of FOXO3 was further enhanced by the constitutively active CAMKIIA mutant.
source: and further enhanced by the constitutively active CAMKIIA mutant (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Expression of Calcineurin significantly inhibited the transcriptional activity of FOXO3.
source: Consistently, expression of Calcineurin significantly inhibited the transcriptional activity of FOXO3 (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 10D.

claim: CAMKIIA and Calcineurin oppose each other in regulating the transcriptional activity of mouse FOXO3 through phosphorylation or dephosphorylation at S298.
source: From these results, we conclude that CAMKIIA and Calcineurin oppose each other in regulating the transcriptional activity of mouse FOXO3 through phosphorylation or dephosphorylation at S298.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of luciferase reporter assays showing opposite effects of CAMKIIA and Calcineurin on FOXO3 activity (Figure 10).

claim: The regulatory mechanism of FOXO by CAMKII and Calcineurin is conserved from C. elegans to mammals.
source: This mechanism is conserved from C. elegans to mammals.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that both C. elegans DAF-16 and mammalian FOXO3 are regulated by CAMKII and Calcineurin at conserved sites (Figures 5-10).

claim: TAX-6 and CNB-1 are expressed in most cells in C. elegans.
source: TAX-6 and CNB-1, similar to DAF-16, are expressed in most cells in C. elegans (Ogg et al., 1997; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2002; Kuhara et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: unc-43 promoter-driven GFP was only detected in neurons and the intestine.
source: In contrast, unc-43 promoter-driven GFP was only detected in neurons and the intestine (Hunt-Newbury et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: UNC-43 was detected primarily in the nervous system.
source: We also detected UNC-43 primarily in the nervous system (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation by the authors.

claim: The TAX-6::GFP fusion protein is distributed diffusely throughout the cytoplasm and inside the nucleus.
source: At the subcellular level, the TAX-6::GFP fusion protein is distributed diffusely throughout the cytoplasm and inside the nucleus (Kuhara et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The CFP::UNC-43 fusion protein is concentrated on perinuclear structures and clusters in neurites.
source: In contrast, the CFP::UNC-43 fusion protein is concentrated on perinuclear structures and clusters in neurites (Umemura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Ca2+-activated CAMKII phosphorylates another molecule of CAMKII at T286 to convert it to a Ca2+/CAM-independent kinase.
source: Temporally, Ca2+-activated CAMKII phosphorylates another molecule of CAMKII at T286 to convert it to a Ca2+/CAM-independent kinase, prolonging the kinase activity after the initial activation (Erickson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CAMKII regulation, supported by citation.

claim: CAMKII can be activated by ROS at low Ca2+ concentrations.
source: CAMKII can also be activated by ROS at low Ca2+ concentrations (Erickson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Human FOXO3 is phosphorylated at non-AKT sites under stress conditions such as heat shock or H2O2 treatment.
source: Reported in HEK293T cells, human FOXO3 is phosphorylated at non-AKT sites under stress conditions such as heat shock or H2O2 treatment (Brunet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: ROS-induced oxidation of two methionine residues activates CAMKII under conditions of low Ca2+.
source: ROS-induced oxidation of two methionine residues activates CAMKII, and this activation can occur under conditions of low Ca2+ (Erickson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of FOXO3 by CAMKII may play a highly conserved role in the stress response, from worms to humans.
source: Thus, CAMKII is perfectly equipped to transmit ROS signaling and calcium signaling, and phosphorylation of FOXO3 by CAMKII may play a highly conserved role in the stress response, from worms to humans.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the conservation of the mechanism and the known functions of CAMKII.

claim: DAF-16 is the only biochemically and genetically proven substrate of TAX-6•CNB-1.
source: To date, DAF-16 is the only biochemically and genetically proven substrate of TAX-6•CNB-1, but it is not the only substrate involved in lifespan regulation by Calcineurin.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of current knowledge.

claim: Inactivation of CRTC-1 contributes to the longevity of tax-6(lf) animals.
source: Inactivation of CRTC-1, a coactivator of CREB, contributes to the longevity of tax-6(lf) animals (Mair et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Post-transplant new-onset diabetes mellitus (NODM) is a frequent and serious complication for organ transplant patients.
source: Post-transplant new-onset diabetes mellitus (NODM) is a frequent and serious complication for organ transplant patients.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: One of the NODM risk factors is the use of Calcineurin inhibitors, such as cyclosporin A and FK506.
source: One of the NODM risk factors is the use of Calcineurin inhibitors, such as cyclosporin A and FK506, which suppress immune-rejection of donor organs (Heisel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Sustained activation of FOXO3 resulting from chronic inhibition of Calcineurin may cause NODM in transplant patients.
source: In light of this work, we propose that sustained activation of FOXO3 resulting from chronic inhibition of Calcineurin may cause NODM in transplant patients.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: The regulatory mechanism uncovered in this study likely plays a role in many physiological functions.
source: Given the conservation and broad tissue distribution of CAMKII, Calcineurin, and FOXO3, the regulatory mechanism uncovered in this study likely plays a role in many physiological functions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the conservation and broad expression of the proteins involved.
